taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO; native to central and southwest Texas into northeastern Mexico.
look_here_first: LOOK HERE FIRST: find the large, coarse, tightly packed perennial CROWN, then follow the tall stalks to long narrow, often densely packed PANICLES. Photograph a complete head and a fresh blade. At the blade–sheath junction, unfold the blade to expose its relatively LONG papery MEMBRANOUS ligule; measure rather than guessing from bunch size or plumage color. Compare a mature single-flowered spikelet and awn with seep muhly; neither species is photo-proven solely by habit.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — UT Plant Resources Center Purola Preserve documents Muhlenbergia lindheimeri in the natural flora. Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed Williamson County treatment. Bell — Flora of North Central Texas documents M. lindheimeri from Bell County and notes its Edwards Plateau distribution.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Landscape-planted ornamental muhly is common; cultivated observations are not used as county-native proof.

best_field_traits: large perennial cespitose bunchgrass, often 100+ stems from the base
upright fountain-form habit, commonly around 1–1.4 m in regional material
narrow stiff blue-green to green blades, usually under about 4 mm wide
very conspicuous membranous ligule, roughly 10–39 mm in the Williamson treatment
tall erect terminal panicle, often 30–60+ cm long and becoming feathery
panicle branches densely flowered and ascending
short awn absent or only a few millimeters long
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Muhlenbergia reverchonii: Seep muhly is much smaller, usually 40–80 cm, with very fine involute blades, shorter ligules, and a more delicate airy reddish panicle. Muhlenbergia capillaris: Pink muhly is widely sold but is not a project-native Central Texas species. Do not identify ornamental pink-plumed muhly as M. lindheimeri by color alone. Muhlenbergia schreberi: Nimblewill is a low weak creeping perennial rooting at lower nodes; Lindheimer muhly is a robust upright basal bunchgrass.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Full scale whole plant and inflorescence plus 10 cm ruler.
Close sheath/ligule with measured membranous margin.
Spikelet macro including glumes, lemma and awn state.
Same-scale flowering head paired with M. reverchonii.
morphology_keys.crew_recognition_note: First check SCALE and the BASAL BUNCH: Lindheimer muhly forms a large coarse, densely tufted fountain often around 0.8–1.5 m tall, with tall relatively contracted, densely flowered panicles. At the leaf collar a LONG MEMBRANOUS ligule is the high-value confirmation; photograph it with a ruler rather than inferring it from plant size.
morphology_keys.precision_caution: Kew GrassBase reports ligules 8–15 mm, and some Williamson County treatments describe broader lengths; do not force a single measurement cutoff on photos. Current sources and external taxon ID remain provisional; existing images show clump and narrow panicles, NOT true ligule or glume.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Compared with M. reverchonii, Lindheimer usually has a much coarser, larger fountainlike crown, larger/stiffer blades, long relatively contracted panicles, and a longer membranous ligule. Kew/GrassBase describes Lindheimer ligules commonly 8–15 mm and seep ligules 2–4(–9) mm, but overlapping treatments mean the actual mature blade/sheath and mature spikelet must agree. The live hybrid M. ×involuta can be intermediate and must NOT be named from intermediate size alone. Nursery M. capillaris (including cultivars) is a separate nonlocal ornamental look-alike, not an acceptable substitute for wild local species photos.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Muhly field check — lindheimeri
steps: WHOLE PLANT: take one level photo of the large upright basal bunch and top of the flowering stalk with ruler/frame-scale; today's first image is habit evidence only.
FLOWERING HEAD: photograph a complete long, narrow often contracted panicle and isolate several attached mature spikelets; today's hand-held photo shows a head, not individual measured florets.

COLLAR: on the SAME plant choose a fully grown blade, gently unfold it at the junction with the surrounding sheath, and photograph the true papery membranous ligule side-on against millimeter scale; compare multiple leaf positions.

LOOK-ALIKES: compare seep muhly's finer tuft and open mature head (that seep head is NOT in these archive photos), then check glumes/lemmas/awn with a lens before calling one of the pair or possible hybrid.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: First check SCALE and the BASAL BUNCH: Lindheimer muhly forms a large coarse, densely tufted fountain often around 0.8–1.5 m tall, with tall relatively contracted, densely flowered panicles. At the leaf collar a LONG MEMBRANOUS ligule is the high-value confirmation; photograph it with a ruler rather than inferring it from plant size.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Published GrassBase ligule ranges (Lindheimer often 8–15 mm; seep 2–4(–9) mm) overlap at some limits. Use multiple characters and a measured mature leaf; all existing arrows identify gross visible growth or seedhead structures only. The seep comparison photo is a DIFFERENT species. The hybrid M. ×involuta must not be inferred from plant size.

Fully unfolded INSIDE of attached leaf junction and long papery ligule with millimeter scale; never arrow unseen ligule.
Several mature spikelets, glumes, lemma tip and actual awn if present, all at 1-mm resolution.

Possible canyon hybrid only when independently verified and documented; intermediate silhouette cannot prove hybrid status.
field_id_finish_pass.comparison_rule: M. reverchonii is usually shorter and finer, with threadlike leaves and a much airier flowering head. M. schreberi has low creeping branching stems that root at nodes. Planted M. capillaris may show pink fluffy flowers but is not automatically the locally native Lindheimer species.

measured_species_key_20261023.look_here_first: Trace a large, densely tufted perennial crown into its tall, often narrow, densely flowered panicle. Open an attached blade/sheath junction and measure the unusually long papery ligule; confirm one-flowered, small awnless-to-short-awned spikelets. Do not identify from plume color alone.
measured_species_key_20261023.growth_form: Strongly cespitose perennial with a dense fibrous crown, commonly many basal stems; culms about 50–150 cm in Kew GrassBase and to 140+ cm in the Williamson County treatment. No extensive rooting surface runners.
measured_species_key_20261023.ligule_collar: Actual eciliate membranous ligule: 8–15 mm in Kew GrassBase; Williamson County documents a membranous portion 10–39 mm, with adjacent sheath-margin lobes to 5 mm. Expose the membrane itself and record the leaf position; neither source range is an absolute exclusion threshold.
measured_species_key_20261023.flowering_architecture: Terminal many-branched panicle, 20–40 cm long and relatively contracted in Kew; Williamson County material describes a 30–62.5 cm long, more open, aging feathery array. Solitary stalked spikelets, each with one fertile floret.
measured_species_key_20261023.spikelet_glume_lemma_awn: Williamson County: mature spikelet 2.5–3.5 mm excluding its short awn; two approximately 2–2.7+ mm, 1-veined membranous glumes, often lower slightly shorter; 3-veined lemma approximately 2 mm, with a terminal awn absent to 4 mm (often 0.1–1.5 mm). Palea approximately 1.8 mm and 2-veined. These are published specimen measurements, NOT measurements verified from installed photos.
measured_species_key_20261023.local_lookalikes: M. reverchonii (seep muhly): smaller, finer basal foliage and a more delicate open panicle; measure ligule and mature spikelets rather than trusting camera-relative size. M. schreberi (nimblewill): weak low stems rooting at nodes, not a tall dense crown. Planted M. capillaris has fluffy pink plumes but is not automatically locally native. M. ×involuta: intermediate habit cannot establish a hybrid without independently reviewed evidence.
